content: Approximately one in three individuals in the United States will develop shingles, also known as herpes zoster, at some point in their lifetime. Shingles can sometimes result in severe complications, such as persistent nerve pain (postherpetic neuralgia) or even vision loss. Vaccination is the most effective way to protect yourself from shingles. Shingles is a painful condition characterized by a rash. It occurs when the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), the same virus responsible for chickenpox, reactivates in the body after a person has previously had chickenpox. Each year, an estimated one million people in the United States are affected by shingles. Most individuals experience shingles only once in their lifetime, but it is possible to have it more than once. The most common presentation of shingles is a rash that appears on one side of the body, either the left or the right. This rash is often accompanied by pain, itching, or a tingling sensation. Shingles can lead to complications, with the most frequent being long-term nerve pain known as postherpetic neuralgia (PHN). You are at risk of developing shingles if you have previously had chickenpox. Over 99% of Americans born before 1980 have had chickenpox, even if they do not recall it. While shingles can occur in children, it is uncommon. The risk of shingles and its complications increases with age, in individuals with weakened immune systems due to medical conditions such as leukemia, lymphoma, or HIV, and in those taking immunosuppressive medications like steroids or drugs used after organ transplants. Shingles is caused by the varicella-zoster virus, which remains dormant in the body after a person has had chickenpox. The virus can reactivate later in life, leading to shingles. It is important to note that you cannot contract shingles directly from someone who has shingles. However, if you have never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine, you can contract chickenpox from someone with shingles. This occurs through direct contact with fluid from the blisters of a shingles rash or by inhaling virus particles from the blisters. Individuals with chickenpox are more contagious than those with shingles. The most effective way to prevent shingles is through vaccination. The CDC recommends two doses of the recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV, Shingrix) for adults aged 50 years and older to prevent shingles and its complications. Shingrix is also recommended for adults aged 19 years and older who have weakened immune systems due to disease or therapy. If you have shingles, you can take steps to protect others from the virus. Covering the rash reduces the risk of spreading the virus. The virus cannot be transmitted before the blisters appear or after the rash has scabbed over. To minimize the risk of transmission, you should cover the rash, avoid touching or scratching it, wash your hands frequently for at least 20 seconds, and avoid contact with certain individuals until the rash has scabbed over. These individuals include pregnant people who have never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine, premature or low birth weight infants, and people with weakened immune systems. Several antiviral medications are available to treat shingles, including acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir. These medications are most effective when taken as soon as the rash appears, as they can reduce the duration and severity of the illness. If you suspect you have shingles, it is important to contact your healthcare provider promptly to discuss treatment options. Pain relief medications, whether over-the-counter or prescribed, can help manage the pain associated with shingles. Additionally, wet compresses, calamine lotion, and warm oatmeal baths may provide relief from itching.
